source: The 400 Investment Banking Interview Questions & Answers You Need to Know

items.prompt_mdx: I see you've done mostly journalism and research internships before. Can you discuss your quantitative skills?

solution.model_answer_mdx:
Pick two or three precise moments where you worked with numbers or logic: a personal portfolio, a maths or science class, a budget you ran, research with data. Say what you computed and what decision came out of it. A claim without a concrete case does not count.

*Personal question: there is no single right answer. Grading here is lenient on purpose; compare your answer with the method above.*

items.prompt_mdx: In your last internship, you analyzed portfolios and recommended investments to clients. Can you walk me through your thought process for analyzing the returns of a client portfolio?

solution.model_answer_mdx:
Break it into numbered steps and stay specific: collect purchase dates and amounts, collect sale dates and proceeds, then aggregate per holding over the period to get a compound return. The interviewer checks that you can explain a process cleanly.

*Personal question: there is no single right answer. Grading here is lenient on purpose; compare your answer with the method above.*

items.prompt_mdx: Can you tell me about the process you used to analyze space requirements for the building designs you worked on this past summer?

solution.model_answer_mdx:
Same logic: steps in order. First estimates, then how you refined them, under which budget constraint and with whom on the team. Show that the numbers became more precise as you went.

*Personal question: there is no single right answer. Grading here is lenient on purpose; compare your answer with the method above.*

items.prompt_mdx: You've been working as a lawyer for the past 3 years, what initiative have you taken on your own to learn more about finance?

solution.model_answer_mdx:
Name what you actually did: courses, a certification such as the CFA, self-study of accounting and valuation, a portfolio you manage, deals you followed from the legal side. Initiative means things you chose to do outside the job.

*Personal question: there is no single right answer. Grading here is lenient on purpose; compare your answer with the method above.*

items.prompt_mdx: You were an English major, how do you know you can handle the quantitative rigor required in investment banking?

solution.model_answer_mdx:
Give evidence instead of reassurance: quantitative classes and grades, test scores, any work with figures, finance self-study. Add that banking needs arithmetic and care with Excel more than advanced maths.

*Personal question: there is no single right answer. Grading here is lenient on purpose; compare your answer with the method above.*

items.prompt_mdx: Can you tell me about a time when you submitted a report or project with misspellings or grammatical mistakes?

solution.model_answer_mdx:
This tests attention to detail. Admit a real but minor slip, then spend most of the answer on what you changed afterwards: a checking routine, printing and rereading, asking a second reader. Claiming it never happened is not credible.

*Personal question: there is no single right answer. Grading here is lenient on purpose; compare your answer with the method above.*

items.prompt_mdx: What's the most number of classes you ever took at once and how well did you do in each of them?

solution.model_answer_mdx:
The real question is workload. Describe your heaviest term, what else you carried alongside (job, activities) and the results. If one grade was weaker, say why and what you did about it.

items.prompt_mdx: What do you do for fun?

solution.model_answer_mdx:
Be honest and specific: one or two real interests, with a detail that makes them memorable. It is a likeability test, so anything genuine beats something meant to impress.

items.prompt_mdx: What was your favorite class in college / business school?
